content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, the garden symbolizes paradise as the place of God's presence and unbroken communion between God and humanity. Rooted in the Garden of Eden, it represents the original blessed state of creation—provision, fellowship with God, and life (the tree of life)—which is lost through sin (expulsion from Eden) and finally restored in the new creation, where Revelation deliberately returns to garden imagery (tree of life, river of life). The garden thus frames the whole canonical arc: paradise created, paradise lost, paradise regained.","primary_basis":["Genesis 2:8-15 (God plants the garden in Eden; tree of life; river)","Genesis 3:8 (God walking in the garden—divine presence)","Genesis 3:23-24 (expulsion from the garden; cherubim guarding the way)","Isaiah 51:3 (Zion's wilderness made like Eden, the garden of the LORD)","Ezekiel 28:13 (Eden, the garden of God)","Ezekiel 36:35 (desolate land becomes like the garden of Eden)","Revelation 2:7 (tree of life in the paradise of God)","Revelation 22:1-5 (river of life, tree of life—Eden restored in the New Jerusalem)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Eden as the archetypal temple or sanctuary: the garden is God's dwelling place, with Adam as priest-guardian; later tabernacle/temple decoration (palm trees, flowers, cherubim) echoes garden imagery. Prominent in modern biblical theology (e.g., G. K. Beale, John Walton) and in some ancient Near Eastern comparative scholarship.","basis":["Genesis 2:15 ('work/serve' and 'keep/guard'—priestly verbs, cf. Numbers 3:7-8)","Genesis 3:24 (cherubim guarding the entrance, as in the tabernacle)","1 Kings 6:29-35 (garden motifs carved in Solomon's temple)","Ezekiel 28:13-14 (Eden linked with the holy mountain of God)","Ezekiel 47:1-12 (river flowing from the temple, echoing Eden's river)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The garden as the bride, and by allegorical extension the Church or the individual soul: the 'enclosed garden' of the Song of Songs was read for centuries (patristic and medieval exegesis; still common in devotional literature) as the Church or the believer's soul in which Christ delights and which he cultivates.","basis":["Song of Songs 4:12-16 ('a garden locked is my sister, my bride')","Song of Songs 5:1; 6:2 (the beloved comes into his garden)","John 15:1-8 (vine and vinedresser imagery often paired with this reading)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The garden as image of the fruitful, Spirit-nourished life of the righteous or of restored Israel—a well-watered garden signifying blessing, flourishing, and spiritual vitality, versus a withered garden signifying judgment.","basis":["Isaiah 58:11 ('you shall be like a watered garden')","Jeremiah 31:12 ('their life shall be like a watered garden')","Isaiah 1:30 (judgment: like a garden without water)","Psalm 1:3 (tree planted by streams of water, thematically linked)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Johannine/new-creation typology: the deliberate garden settings of Jesus' passion and resurrection (Gethsemane, the garden tomb, Mary mistaking Jesus for 'the gardener') portray Christ as the new Adam undoing Eden's fall and inaugurating new creation. Widely noted in commentaries and preaching, though it is a typological reading rather than a stated biblical definition.","basis":["John 18:1 (arrest in a garden)","John 19:41 (garden tomb, new tomb)","John 20:15 (Mary supposes him to be the gardener)","Romans 5:12-21; 1 Corinthians 15:45 (Adam-Christ typology supplying the framework)"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The garden as the human heart to be cultivated—a devotional/homiletical application in which weeds are sins and cultivation is sanctification. Popular in sermons and devotional writing but not a formal exegetical tradition.","basis":["Matthew 13:3-23 (parable of the sower, soils of the heart)","Song of Songs 4:12 (applied to the soul)","Galatians 5:22-23 (fruit of the Spirit, thematically invoked)"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad, recognizable consensus that the garden's primary symbolic register is Eden/paradise—the place of God's presence and communion with humanity, lost through sin and restored eschatologically (Genesis 2-3 to Revelation 22). The main alternative readings (temple-sanctuary, bride/Church/soul, watered-garden fruitfulness, Johannine new-creation typology) are largely complementary layers rather than rival meanings, which is why they are widespread without displacing the primary sense. The temple reading is dominant in recent academic biblical theology but is best classed as 'common' across Christian teaching overall; the bridal/soul allegory was dominant in premodern exegesis of the Song of Songs but is less central today."}
